bibl.title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Measurement of equity risk premia, treated as a prediction problem, across the machine learning method repertoire.
span.quote: we conduct a comparative analysis of machine learning methods for finance. We do so in the context of perhaps the most widely studied problem in finance, that of measuring equity risk premia.

span.label: How do machine learning methods compare for the canonical problem of empirical asset pricing, measuring asset risk premia?
span.quote: We perform a comparative analysis of machine learning methods for the canonical problem of empirical asset pricing: measuring asset risk premia.

span.label: Provides benchmarks for the predictive accuracy of machine learning methods in measuring risk premia, robust across specifications.
span.quote: we provide a new set of benchmarks for the predictive accuracy of machine learning methods in measuring risk premia of the aggregate market and individual stocks. This accuracy is summarized two ways. The first is a high out-of-sample predictive R2 relative to preceding literature that is robust across a variety of machine learning specifications.

span.label: method
span.quote: We identify the best performing methods (trees and neural networks) and trace their predictive gains to allowance of nonlinear predictor interactions

span.label: trees and neural networks improve return prediction over linear and generalized linear models, traced to their allowance of interactions among predictors
span.quote: We find that trees and neural networks unambiguously improve return prediction with monthly stock-level R2's between 0.33% and 0.40%. But the generalized linear model, which introduces nonlinearity via spline functions of each individual baseline predictor (but with no predictor interactions), fails to robustly outperform the linear specification. This suggests that allowing for (potentially complex) interactions among the baseline predictors is a crucial aspect of nonlinearities in the expected return function.

span.label: comparative empirical analysis
span.quote: We conduct a large scale empirical analysis, investigating nearly 30,000 individual stocks over 60 years from 1957 to 2016. Our predictor set includes 94 characteristics for each stock, interactions of each characteristic with eight aggregate time series variables, and 74 industry sector dummy variables, totaling more than 900 baseline signals.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the sample is cut into three disjoint periods that keep the data's time ordering: the model is estimated on the training period alone, while the hyperparameters are chosen by scoring forecasts on the second period and re-estimating from the training data at every step
span.quote: In particular, we divide our sample into three disjoint time periods that maintain the temporal ordering of the data. The first, or "training," subsample is used to estimate the model subject to a specific set of tuning parameter values. The second, or "validation," sample is used for tuning the hyperparameters. We construct forecasts for data points in the validation sample based on the estimated model from the training sample. Next, we calculate the objective function based on forecast errors from the validation sample, and iteratively search for hyperparameters that optimize the validation objective (at each step re-estimating the model from the training data subject to the prevailing hyperparameter values). Tuning parameters are chosen from the validation sample taking into account estimated parameters, but the parameters are estimated from the training data alone.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the third period is used for neither estimation nor tuning, which is what makes it the only one of the three that is truly out of sample - the validation fits are not, because they are an input to the estimation
span.quote: Thus the third, or "testing," subsample, which is used for neither estimation nor tuning, is truly out-of-sample and thus is used to evaluate a method's predictive performance.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the out-of-sample R-squared is computed against a forecast of zero rather than against the historical mean return, because the historical mean of an individual stock is so noisy that benchmarking against it would lower the bar - and the paper states the size of the choice: every method's monthly R-squared rises by roughly three percentage points under the conventional denominator
span.quote: A subtle but important aspect of our R2 metric is that the denominator is the sum of squared excess returns without demeaning. In many out-of-sample forecasting applications, predictions are compared against historical mean returns. While this approach is sensible for the aggregate index or long-short portfolios, for example, it is flawed when it comes to analyzing individual stock returns. Predicting future excess stock returns with historical averages typically underperforms a naive fore- cast of zero by a large margin. That is, the historical mean stock return is so noisy that it artificially lowers the bar for "good" forecasting performance. We avoid this pitfall by benchmarking our R2 against a forecast value of zero. To give an indication of the importance of this choice, when we benchmark model predictions against historical mean stock returns, the out-of-sample monthly R2 of all methods rises by roughly three percentage points.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the Diebold-Mariano comparison is applied to the cross-sectional AVERAGE of each month's prediction errors rather than to individual stock errors, because the test's weak-dependence condition is unlikely to hold across a cross-section of stocks with potentially strong dependence
span.quote: While time series dependence in returns is sufficiently weak, it is unlikely that the conditions of weak error dependence underlying the Diebold-Mariano test apply to our stock-level analysis due of potentially strong dependence in the cross section. We adapt Diebold-Mariano to our setting by comparing the cross-sectional average of prediction errors from each model, instead of comparing errors among individual returns.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the network architectures are fixed in advance instead of searched over, because searching uncountably many is called unrealistic and unnecessary - and what the authors say they hope to obtain is a reasonable LOWER BOUND on machine-learning performance, not the best network
span.quote: It is unrealistic and unnecessary to find the optimal network by searching over uncountably many architectures. Instead, we fix a variety of network architectures ex ante and estimate each of these. What we hope to achieve is reasonably lower bound on the performance of machine learning methods.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the squared-error objective is replaced by a hybrid of squared loss for relatively small errors and absolute loss for relatively large ones, with the crossover controlled by a tuning parameter optimised adaptively from the data
span.note: about this quote: Q-609, 2026-08-16: THE EXTRACTION HAS STRIPPED THE MATH SYMBOLS INSIDE THIS QUOTE. It reads "The Huber loss, H(?), is a hybrid ... controlled by a tuning parameter, , that can be optimized adaptively" - the argument of H and the NAME OF THE TUNING PARAMETER are both absent from the staged file, leaving a bare comma where the symbol was. The quote is an exact substring and the file is incomplete here. The tag deliberately describes the parameter by its role rather than naming it, because naming it would mean supplying a character the staged text does not contain.
span.quote: The Huber loss, H(�), is a hybrid of squared loss for relatively small errors and absolute loss for relatively large errors, where the combination is controlled by a tuning parameter, , that can be optimized adaptively from the data.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: trees in the forest are de-correlated by offering each branch only a randomly drawn subset of the predictors, so that a single dominant predictor cannot force the same early split in every bootstrap sample and collapse the variance reduction that averaging is supposed to provide
span.quote: The forest method de-correlates trees using a method known as "dropout," which considers only a randomly drawn subset of predictors for splitting at each potential branch. Doing so ensures that, in the example, early branches for at least a few trees will split on characteristics other than firm size. This lowers the average correlation among predictions to further improve the variance reduction relative to standard bagging.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the network is estimated from several different random initialisations and the forecasts are averaged, because the optimiser is stochastic and a single seed's forecast carries variance that has nothing to do with the data
span.quote: In particular, we use multiple random seeds to initialize neural network estimation and construct predictions by averaging forecasts from all networks. This reduces prediction variance because the stochastic nature of the optimization can cause different seeds to produce different forecasts.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the interpretation of which methods win is checked against two simulated data sets whose generating processes are known - one linear and additive, one nonlinear with pairwise interactions - so that the ranking can be shown to track the property it is being credited to
span.quote: We apply machine learning to simulated data from two different data generating processes. Both produce data from a high dimensional predictor set. But in one, individual predictors enter only linearly and additively, while in the other predictors can enter through nonlinear transformations and via pairwise interactions. When we apply our machine learning repertoire to the simulated datasets, we find that linear and generalized linear methods dominate in the linear and uninteracted setting, yet tree-based methods and neural networks significantly outperform in the nonlinear and interactive setting.

span.label: The headline R2 uses a denominator without demeaning; the paper states the common alternative convention raises every method's R2 by roughly three percentage points.
span.note: what this limits: comparing this paper's R2 against an R2 computed the usual way, against historical mean returns: the paper says that convention raises all its numbers by roughly three percentage points
span.quote: A subtle but important aspect of our R2 metric is that the denominator is the sum of squared excess returns without demeaning. In many out-of-sample forecasting applications, predictions are compared against historical mean returns. While this approach is sensible for the aggregate index or long-short portfolios, for example, it is flawed when it comes to analyzing individual stock returns. Predicting future excess stock returns with historical averages typically underperforms a naive fore- cast of zero by a large margin. That is, the historical mean stock return is so noisy that it artificially lowers the bar for "good" forecasting performance. We avoid this pitfall by benchmarking our R2 against a forecast value of zero. To give an indication of the importance of this choice, when we benchmark model predictions against historical mean stock returns, the out-of-sample monthly R2 of all methods rises by roughly three percentage points.

span.label: The paper states its improved predictions are measurements only, and do not identify economic mechanisms or equilibria.
span.note: what this limits: reading the results as evidence about economic mechanisms: the paper says the measurements do not tell us about mechanisms or equilibria
span.quote: But these improved predictions are only measurements. The measurements do not tell us about economic mechanisms or equilibria. Machine learning methods on their own do not identify deep fundamental associations among asset prices and conditioning variables.

span.label: The set of methods compared is explicitly not exhaustive, and support vector machines are excluded with a stated reason.
span.note: what this limits: reading the comparison as covering the machine learning toolkit: the paper says it is not exhaustive and names an exclusion
span.quote: This is not an exhaustive analysis of all methods. For example, we exclude support vector machines as these share an equivalence with other methods that we study4 and are primarily used for classification problems.

span.label: The paper describes its own interpretive goal as modest.
span.note: what this limits: reading the variable-importance results as an account of why a predictor works: the stated goal is only to identify influential covariates
span.quote: Our goal in interpreting machine learning models is modest. We aim to identify covariates that have an important influence on the cross-section of expected returns while simultaneously controlling for the many other predictors in the system.

span.label: The conditions underlying the Diebold-Mariano test are stated to be unlikely to hold for the stock-level analysis; the paper modifies the test rather than proceeding.
span.note: what this limits: the reported model-comparison p-values as standard Diebold-Mariano results: the test was adapted because its conditions were judged unlikely to hold
span.quote: it is unlikely that the conditions of weak error dependence underlying the Diebold-Mariano test apply to our stock-level analysis due of potentially strong dependence in the cross section. We adapt Diebold-Mariano to our setting by comparing the cross-sectional average of prediction errors from each model, instead of comparing errors among individual returns.

span.label: The predictor literature the study draws on is stated to exclude an unknown larger set of predictors that were tested, failed and never reported.
span.note: what this limits: the 900+ signal set as the space of tested predictors: the paper says an unknown larger set failed and was never reported
span.quote: In both stock and aggregate return predictions, there presumably exists a much larger set of predictors that were tested but failed to predict returns and were thus never reported.

span.label: The finding that shallow networks beat deeper ones is attributed, with hedging, to the data available rather than established as a property of the problem.
span.note: what this limits: generalising shallow-beats-deep beyond this setting: the paper attributes it, hedged, to the small data and low signal-to-noise ratio here
span.quote: This is likely an artifact of the relatively small amount of data and tiny signal-to-noise ratio for our return prediction problem, in comparison to the kinds of non-financial settings in which deep learning thrives thanks to astronomical datasets and strong signals (such as computer vision).

span.label: The estimation target is defined in terms of an information set the paper calls true and unobservable.
span.note: what this limits: treating the target as an observable quantity: the conditioning information set is stated to be unobservable
span.quote: It amounts to best approximating the conditional expectation E(ri,t+1|Ft), where ri,t+1 is an asset's return in excess of the risk-free rate, and Ft is the true and unobservable information set of market participants.

span.label: The paper's central term is stated to have no settled definition, and the definition used is stipulated by the authors.
span.note: what this limits: reading "machine learning" here as a standard term: the paper says the definition is inchoate and stipulates its own three-part one
span.quote: The definition of "machine learning" is inchoate and is often context specific. We use the term to describe (i) a diverse collection of high-dimensional models for statistical prediction, combined with (ii) so-called "regularization" methods for model selection and mitigation of overfit, and (iii) efficient algorithms for searching among a vast number of potential model specifications.

span.label: the architecture and vocabulary of the biological nervous system - neurons, synapses, axons, signals passed between layers - carried into empirical asset pricing as the description of a feed-forward network
span.quote: Analogous to axons in a biological brain, layers of the networks represent groups of "neurons" with each layer connected by "synapses" that transmit signals among neurons of different layers.

span.label: parameter penalisation and deliberately conservative model-selection criteria applied across the whole method comparison
span.note: eliminates: overfitting and false discovery as the source of apparent predictive power - the flexible functional forms being compared can fit noise, and without the penalty the comparison would reward whichever method fits it best
span.quote: parameter penalization and conservative model selection criteria complement the breadth of functional forms spanned by these methods in order to avoid overfit biases and false discovery

span.label: machine learning
span.quote: The definition of "machine learning" is inchoate and is often context specific.

span.label: risk premium
span.quote: We use the terms "expected return" and "risk premium" interchangeably.

span.label: expected return
span.quote: Our focus is on measuring conditional expected stock returns in excess of the risk-free rate.

span.label: neural networks
span.quote: When we consider a range of neural networks from very shallow (a single hidden layer) to deeper networks (up to five hidden layers), we find that neural network performance peaks at three hidden layers then declines as more layers are added.

span.label: regression trees
span.quote: we expand the model to accommodate nonlinear predictive relationships via generalized linear models, regression trees, and neural networks.

span.label: elastic net
span.quote: the "elastic net," which uses parameter shrinkage and variable selection to limit the regression's degrees of freedom, solves the OLS inefficiency problem.

span.label: support vector machines
span.quote: we exclude support vector machines as these share an equivalence with other methods that we study4 and are primarily used for classification problems.

span.label: variable importance
span.quote: We discover influential covariates by ranking them according to a notion of variable importance

span.quote: A subtle but important aspect of our R2 metric is that the denominator is the sum of squared excess returns without demeaning.

span.label: predictive performance
span.quote: To assess predictive performance for individual excess stock return forecasts, we calculate the outof-sample R2 as

span.label: traditional econometric prediction techniques
span.quote: enhances their flexibility relative to more traditional econometric prediction techniques.

span.label: Diebold-Mariano test
span.quote: To make pairwise comparisons of methods, we use the Diebold and Mariano (1995) test for differences in out-of-sample predictive accuracy between two models.

span.label: out-of-sample R2 - denominator is the sum of squared excess returns, NOT demeaned, so the benchmark forecast is zero
span.quote: A subtle but important aspect of our R2 metric is that the denominator is the sum of squared excess returns without demeaning. In many out-of-sample forecasting applications, predictions are compared against historical mean returns. While this approach is sensible for the aggregate index or long-short portfolios, for example, it is flawed when it comes to analyzing individual stock returns. Predicting future excess stock returns with historical averages typically underperforms a naive fore- cast of zero by a large margin. That is, the historical mean stock return is so noisy that it artificially lowers the bar for "good" forecasting performance. We avoid this pitfall by benchmarking our R2 against a forecast value of zero.

span.label: out-of-sample R2 - the conventional sense, benchmarked against historical mean returns, which the paper says would raise all its numbers by about three percentage points
span.quote: In many out-of-sample forecasting applications, predictions are compared against historical mean returns. While this approach is sensible for the aggregate index or long-short portfolios, for example, it is flawed when it comes to analyzing individual stock returns. Predicting future excess stock returns with historical averages typically underperforms a naive fore- cast of zero by a large margin. That is, the historical mean stock return is so noisy that it artificially lowers the bar for "good" forecasting performance. We avoid this pitfall by benchmarking our R2 against a forecast value of zero. To give an indication of the importance of this choice, when we benchmark model predictions against historical mean stock returns, the out-of-sample monthly R2 of all methods rises by roughly three percentage points.

span.label: machine learning - the authors' stipulated three-part sense: high-dimensional prediction models, regularization, and search algorithms
span.quote: We use the term to describe (i) a diverse collection of high-dimensional models for statistical prediction, combined with (ii) so-called "regularization" methods for model selection and mitigation of overfit, and (iii) efficient algorithms for searching among a vast number of potential model specifications.

span.label: risk premium - used interchangeably with expected return, while the paper notes components one may wish to distinguish
span.quote: We use the terms "expected return" and "risk premium" interchangeably. One may be interested in potentially distinguishing among different components of expected returns such as those due to systematic risk compensation, idiosyncratic risk compensation, or even due to mispricing.

span.label: variable importance - a ranking used to identify influential covariates, explicitly not an account of mechanism
span.quote: Our goal in interpreting machine learning models is modest. We aim to identify covariates that have an important influence on the cross-section of expected returns while simultaneously controlling for the many other predictors in the system.

span.label: qualifies → Green et al. (2013), Harvey et al. (2016), Welch and Goyal (2008) — the predictor-counting literature
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE COUNT IS OF PREDICTORS OR OF REPORTED PREDICTORS. Three surveys are cited with their totals - 330 stock-level signals, 316 factors, nearly 20 aggregate-market predictors - and then: 'THERE PRESUMABLY EXISTS A MUCH LARGER SET OF PREDICTORS THAT WERE TESTED BUT FAILED TO PREDICT RETURNS AND WERE THUS NEVER REPORTED.' The denominator of the search is unobservable, so the counts bound the published literature and not the work done
span.quote: Green et al. (2013) count 330 stock-level predictive signals in published or circulated drafts. Harvey et al. (2016) study 316 "factors," which include firm characteristics and common factors, for describing stock return behavior. They note that this is only a subset of those studied in the literature. Welch and Goyal (2008) analyze nearly 20 predictors for the aggregate market return. In both stock and aggregate return predictions, there presumably exists a much larger set of predictors that were tested but failed to predict returns and were thus never reported.

span.label: builds-on → Welch and Goyal (2008)
span.note: differs in: WHAT THE BENCHMARK IS. The comparison point is not a rival method's success but a documented FAILURE: 'nearly all of the macroeconomic return predictor variables in the survey of Welch and Goyal (2008) FAIL TO PRODUCE A POSITIVE OUT-OF-SAMPLE FORECAST R2.' A negative result is doing the work of a baseline, which is only legible if the reader knows the sign convention of this R2 - and the record already carries two senses of it
span.quote: As a benchmark for comparison, nearly all of the macroeconomic return predictor variables in the survey of Welch and Goyal (2008) fail to produce a positive out-of-sample forecast R2.

span.label: distinguishes-from → principal components regression (PCA)
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE DIMENSION REDUCTION KNOWS WHAT IT IS PREDICTING. 'PCA condenses data into components based on the covariation AMONG THE PREDICTORS. THIS HAPPENS PRIOR TO THE FORECASTING STEP AND WITHOUT CONSIDERATION OF HOW PREDICTORS ASSOCIATE WITH FUTURE RETURNS. IN CONTRAST, partial least squares performs dimension reduction by DIRECTLY EXPLOITING COVARIATION OF PREDICTORS WITH THE FORECAST TARGET.' Two reductions of the same data differing only in whether the target is in scope when the axes are chosen
span.quote: PCA condenses data into components based on the covariation among the predictors. This happens prior to the forecasting step and without consideration of how predictors associate with future returns. In contrast, partial least squares performs dimension reduction by directly exploiting covariation of predictors with the forecast target.

span.label: risk premium —same-as→ expected return
span.quote: We use the terms "expected return" and "risk premium" interchangeably.

span.quote: To assess predictive performance for individual excess stock return forecasts, we calculate the outof-sample R2 as

span.label: neural networks —contrasted-with→ regression trees
span.quote: Neural networks and, to a lesser extent, regression trees, are the best performing methods.

span.label: support vector machines —part-of→ machine learning
span.quote: our list is designed to be representative of predictive analytics tools from various branches of the machine learning toolkit.

span.label: machine learning —contrasted-with→ traditional econometric prediction techniques
span.quote: The high-dimensional nature of machine learning methods (element (i) of this definition) enhances their flexibility relative to more traditional econometric prediction techniques
